full_title: ATTY. CARMEN CARMELA A. ARAULLO-ANTIPORTA, CLERK OF COURT VI, REGIONAL TRIAL COURT, OFFICE OF THE CLERK OF COURT, MANDAUE CITY, CEBU, COMPLAINANT, VS. ATTY. DENIS L. PACAS, CLERK OF COURT V, BRANCH 54, REGIONAL TRIAL COURT, LAPU-LAPU CITY, CEBU AND ANTHONY PACALDO, SHERIFF IV, BRANCH 84, REGIONAL TRIAL COURT, MANDAUE CITY, CEBU [FORMERLY CLERK III, BRANCH 54, REGIONAL TRIAL COURT, LAPU-LAPU CITY, CEBU], RESPONDENTS.
subject: Remedial Law, Legal and Judicial Ethics
syllabus_topic: IX. Legal and Judicial Ethics > B. Judicial Ethics (CJCA) > 2. Accountability of Members of the Judiciary > a. Judicial Accountability and Disciplinary Proceedings (Canon VII)
topics: Gross neglect of duty: case records lost and untransmitted for over eight years
Gross insubordination: repeated disregard of superiors' directives
Branch clerk of court's liability for failure to supervise (simple neglect)
Locally funded employees may not have custody of court records
Rule 140 penalties; admonition and warning are not aggravating circumstances

other_subjects.subject: Political and Public International Law
other_subjects.syllabus_topic: XI. Law on Public Officers > D. Accountability of Public Officers (RA 6713) > 2. Discipline > a. Grounds

doctrine:
**A court employee directly charged with the custody and transmittal of case records who lets them go missing and untransmitted for more than eight years, without informing his superior or genuinely trying to locate them, is guilty of gross neglect of duty.** This is a serious charge under Rule 140, Section 14(d), as amended by A.M. No. 21-08-09-SC. Such neglect threatens the public welfare, particularly the accused's right to a speedy disposition of his case. **Repeatedly ignoring superiors' directives without valid justification is gross insubordination** (Sec. 14(n)). Here the directives were to inventory cases, update the docket book, locate missing records, and turn over records before moving to a new post. A heavy workload is a "flimsy excuse."

**The branch clerk of court is liable for simple neglect of duty, a less serious charge (Sec. 15(b)), even if a subordinate was directly at fault.** As the official custodian of court records (Rule 136, Sec. 7) with general supervision over court personnel, his responsibility does not end when he delegates a task. He must ensure that his instruction is carried out and keep an effective record management system with periodic inventories. Clerks of court are chiefly responsible for the shortcomings of subordinates to whom their administrative functions are delegated (*Baring-Uy v. Salinas*). Locally funded employees detailed to lower courts may do only clerical work and may not be given custody of records (OCA Circular No. 42-2019), so blaming such an employee does not prosper.

On penalties (Rule 140, Secs. 17, 19 and 20, as amended): when there are one or more mitigating circumstances and no aggravating circumstance, the Court may impose a suspension or fine of not less than half of the prescribed minimum. A first offense, and humanitarian considerations such as remorse, apology and prompt remedial action, are mitigating. **An earlier admonition or warning is not a penalty and cannot be treated as an aggravating circumstance.** Each offense was penalized separately.
facts:
On June 29, 2012, Judge Victor A. Teves, Sr. directed the transmittal of the records of Criminal Case Nos. 018271-L, 018272-L and 018273-L (People v. Ceasar R. Baguio, for violation of Sections 5, 11 and 12 of RA 9165) to the Office of the Clerk of Court (OCC), RTC Mandaue City. The records reached the OCC only on November 24, 2020. Only the original records of Criminal Case No. 018271-L were delivered; machine copies of the other two had to be obtained from the Office of the Provincial Prosecutor. Complainant Atty. Araullo-Antiporta, Clerk of Court VI of the OCC, reported this in a December 7, 2020 letter, which was endorsed to the OCA and forwarded to the Judicial Integrity Board (JIB).

Branch Clerk of Court Atty. Denis L. Pacas's investigation report stated that the transmittal was the task of respondent Anthony Pacaldo, then clerk-in-charge of criminal cases. When confronted, Pacaldo said he could not find the records. The court interpreter later found the original records of Criminal Case No. 018271-L in a pile of folders under Pacaldo's table. Pacaldo denied receiving the instruction. He claimed it was given to Teofilo Bering, a locally funded employee detailed to Branch 54, who died in 2013. Atty. Pacas submitted affidavits of the accused's wife (who followed up with Pacaldo in 2012-2013) and of a jail records officer (who exchanged calls and texts with Pacaldo since 2019), and a sheriff's memorandum. All showed that Pacaldo had said the records could not be found. Pacaldo had also received memoranda since 2011 about inventories, the docket book, missing records and absences from his station. He did not comply with a 2020 directive to inventory and turn over his records before moving to his new post as sheriff, citing his workload. Atty. Pacas apologized and acted promptly, and the original records were eventually delivered on December 10, 2021.

The JIB's Office of the Executive Director recommended a finding of simple neglect against Pacaldo (fine of PHP 18,000) and dismissal of the case against Atty. Pacas with a stern warning. The JIB instead found both guilty of gross neglect of duty and Pacaldo also guilty of gross insubordination. It recommended a PHP 75,000 fine for Atty. Pacas, treating an earlier administrative matter as an aggravating circumstance, and a four-month suspension plus a PHP 55,000 fine for Pacaldo.
issues: Whether Pacaldo, the former clerk-in-charge of criminal cases, is guilty of gross neglect of duty and gross insubordination.
Whether Atty. Pacas, the branch clerk of court, is administratively liable even though Pacaldo was directly responsible for the delay.
What penalties are proper in light of the modifying circumstances.
ruling:
The Court adopted the JIB's findings with modifications.

**1. Yes, Pacaldo is guilty of both.** The records were transmitted more than eight years after the judge's order. As clerk-in-charge of criminal cases, Pacaldo was directly responsible. The affidavits and memoranda of court staff, the jail records officer and the accused's wife showed that he knew of the task: they repeatedly followed up with him, and he told them the records could not be found. His claim that Bering received the instruction was an afterthought, since Bering had died in 2013 and could not refute it. It was also contrary to OCA Circular No. 42-2019, which bars locally funded employees from custody of records. Absent contrary proof, Atty. Pacas is presumed to have properly directed Pacaldo. Pacaldo made no genuine effort to locate the records or inform his superior, and his neglect threatened the accused's right to a speedy disposition of his case. That is **gross neglect of duty**. He also ignored his superiors' memoranda since 2011 and the 2020 directive to inventory and turn over his records, citing a heavy workload. This repeated, unjustified defiance is **gross insubordination**.

**2. Yes, Atty. Pacas is guilty of simple neglect of duty.** As branch clerk of court he exercises general supervision over court personnel and is the official custodian of court records. His responsibility "did not terminate when he delegated its transmittal" to Pacaldo; he had to make sure his instruction was complied with. He "blindly depended" on Pacaldo and failed to put in place an effective case management system and periodic inventory, which would have exposed the problem much earlier. Clerks of court are chiefly responsible for the shortcomings of subordinates to whom their functions are delegated (*Baring-Uy v. Salinas*). His lapse was carelessness, amounting to simple, not gross, neglect.

**3. The penalties were adjusted.** Gross neglect of duty and gross insubordination are serious charges, punishable by dismissal, suspension of more than six months up to one year, or a fine of more than PHP 100,000 up to PHP 200,000 (Sec. 17(1)). Simple neglect is a less serious charge, punishable by suspension of one to six months or a fine of more than PHP 35,000 up to PHP 100,000 (Sec. 17(2)). Under Section 20, when there are mitigating and no aggravating circumstances, the penalty may be not less than half of the minimum.

This was Pacaldo's first administrative charge, a mitigating circumstance. For gross neglect, the Court adopted the JIB's recommended four-month suspension. For gross insubordination, "without the benefit of any mitigating circumstance," it suspended him for six months and one day. Atty. Pacas was credited with humanitarian considerations: he apologized, acted immediately, secured certified copies of the missing records, and kept searching until the originals were delivered. **The Court rejected the JIB's use of his earlier admonition and stern warning in a judicial audit as an aggravating circumstance, because admonition and warning are not penalties.** He was fined PHP 18,000, payable within 30 days from finality (*Ignacio v. Balading*).
disposition: Pacaldo was found GUILTY of gross neglect of duty in the performance of official functions and SUSPENDED for four months without salary or other benefits. He was also found GUILTY of gross insubordination and SUSPENDED for six months and one day without salary or other benefits. Atty. Pacas was found GUILTY of simple neglect of duty in the performance of official functions and FINED PHP 18,000, payable within 30 days from finality; if unpaid, contempt proceedings under Rule 71, Section 3 will be commenced. Both were STERNLY WARNED that a repetition will be dealt with more severely. A copy was furnished to the OCA.

bar_questions.q: In 2015, Judge Lim ordered the records of three criminal cases transmitted to the Office of the Clerk of Court. Branch Clerk of Court Atty. Rey assigned the task to Joel, the clerk-in-charge of criminal cases, and never followed up. Joel could not find the records. For years he told the accused's relatives that the records were "still being located," but he never informed Atty. Rey and never seriously searched. The records were transmitted only in 2023. What are the administrative liabilities of Joel and Atty. Rey?

alac.answer: Joel is liable for gross neglect of duty, a serious charge. Atty. Rey is liable for simple neglect of duty, a less serious charge.
alac.legal_basis: Gross neglect of duty is negligence marked by a glaring want of care, or a flagrant and culpable refusal or unwillingness to perform a duty; it is a serious charge under Rule 140, Section 14(d), as amended by A.M. No. 21-08-09-SC. Simple neglect is the failure to give attention to an expected task through carelessness or indifference (Sec. 15(b)). The branch clerk of court is the official custodian of records (Rule 136, Sec. 7) and supervises court personnel. He remains responsible after delegating a task and is chiefly answerable for his subordinates' shortcomings. (Araullo-Antiporta v. Pacas, JIB FPI No. 21-006-P, August 4, 2025)
alac.application: Joel was directly in charge of the records and knew of the task, since he answered the relatives' follow-ups. Yet for about eight years he neither searched seriously nor told his superior, which delayed the cases and threatened the accused's right to a speedy disposition. That is gross neglect. Atty. Rey did not lose the records himself, but he delegated the task and never checked whether it was done, and he had no system or inventory that would have revealed the loss. His failure to supervise is carelessness, which is simple neglect.
alac.conclusion: Joel should be held liable for gross neglect of duty and Atty. Rey for simple neglect of duty.

bar_questions.q: In the same case, Joel raises two defenses. (a) He says the judge's instruction was actually given to a job-order employee funded by the municipality and detailed to the branch, who has since died. (b) He admits ignoring the judge's memorandum to inventory his records and turn them over before transferring to his new post as sheriff, but blames his heavy workload in the new post. He has also received several earlier memoranda about his failure to update the docket book and locate missing records. Rule on his defenses.

alac.answer: Both defenses fail. Joel remains liable for gross neglect of duty and is also liable for gross insubordination.
alac.legal_basis: Under OCA Circular No. 42-2019, locally funded employees detailed to lower courts may perform only clerical tasks and may not be given custody of court records. Absent contrary proof, the branch clerk is presumed to have regularly performed his duty of assigning the task to the proper employee. Gross insubordination is the inexplicable and unjustified refusal to obey an order that a superior is entitled to give, importing a willful disregard of lawful and reasonable instructions; it is a serious charge under Rule 140, Section 14(n). (Araullo-Antiporta v. Pacas, JIB FPI No. 21-006-P, August 4, 2025)
alac.application: (a) Blaming a deceased employee who cannot refute the claim is an afterthought. It is also implausible, since such an employee could not lawfully have been given custody of the records, and Joel offers no proof beyond his own word. (b) Joel repeatedly ignored lawful directives from the judge and the branch clerk, and a heavy workload is a flimsy excuse for not inventorying and turning over records in his custody. His persistent disregard of his superiors' orders is gross insubordination.
alac.conclusion: Joel's defenses should be rejected; he is liable for both gross neglect of duty and gross insubordination.

bar_questions.q: In determining Atty. Rey's penalty for simple neglect of duty, the Judicial Integrity Board treated as an aggravating circumstance a ruling in an earlier judicial audit, where Atty. Rey was admonished and sternly warned for late docket inventories. Atty. Rey points out that he apologized, immediately secured certified copies of the missing records from the prosecutor's office, and kept searching until the originals were found. (a) Was the JIB correct in treating the earlier admonition as aggravating? (b) May the Court impose a penalty lower than the minimum for a less serious charge?

alac.answer: (a) No. An admonition and a warning are not penalties, so they cannot aggravate his liability. (b) Yes. With a mitigating circumstance and no aggravating circumstance, the Court may impose a fine of not less than half of the minimum.
alac.legal_basis: Under Rule 140, Sections 19 and 20, as amended by A.M. No. 21-08-09-SC, humanitarian considerations are a mitigating circumstance. When one or more mitigating circumstances and no aggravating circumstance are present, the Court may impose a suspension or fine of not less than half of the minimum prescribed. Admonition and warning are not penalties and cannot be treated as an aggravating circumstance. (Araullo-Antiporta v. Pacas, JIB FPI No. 21-006-P, August 4, 2025)
alac.application: Because the earlier ruling merely admonished and warned Atty. Rey, it imposed no penalty, so there is no aggravating circumstance. His apology, his immediate remedial action, and his persistence until the originals were found are humanitarian considerations that mitigate his liability. With one mitigating and no aggravating circumstance, the Court may reduce his fine below the minimum for a less serious charge, as long as it is not less than half of that minimum.
alac.conclusion: The prior admonition is not aggravating, and Atty. Rey may be fined below the minimum, but not less than half of it, because of the mitigating circumstance.

notes:
First Division Resolution. Gesmundo, C.J. (Chairperson) and Hernando, J. concurred; Zalameda and Marquez, JJ. were on official business. The JIB acted on the endorsed letter on its own, as Rule 140, as amended by A.M. No. 21-08-09-SC, allows.

The Resolution applied Rule 140 as amended by A.M. No. 21-08-09-SC. The 2027 syllabus refers to the 2025 CJCA and the 2025 Code of Conduct and Accountability for Court Officials and Personnel (A.M. No. 25-06-11-SC), so check whether later rules changed the classification of these offenses or the sanctions. The syllabus has no separate heading for the discipline of court personnel; the closest heading is used. The Resolution does not explain why the first-offense mitigating circumstance was applied only to the gross neglect charge and not to gross insubordination.
